content: Public health authorities, aviation authorities, and other stakeholders must remain informed and anticipate the potential consequences of regulatory changes that could impact the use of chemicals across various jurisdictions. Airlines are required to notify passengers and cargo customers at the time of booking if aircraft disinsection is mandated for flights to or from their destination. Countries should provide clear and accessible information to aircraft operators upon request, explaining national regulations, the rationale for disinsection requirements, and the safety of properly conducted disinsection procedures. Airlines must adhere to national regulations regarding the storage and disposal of used insecticide containers. Aircraft disinsection methods and insecticides must comply with the requirements of both the country where the treatment is applied and the country of arrival. Pre-embarkation and pre-departure methods have replaced pre-flight and top-of-descent cabin treatments. Pre-embarkation cabin disinsection involves aerosol spraying of the aircraft cabin before passengers board, ensuring the treatment is effective for a single flight sector. This method eliminates mosquitoes and other vectors present at the time of disinsection and leaves a minimal but effective residue to kill vectors that may board before departure. Surfaces must be cleaned and dried before treatment, and the procedure must be conducted after catering is completed and service doors are closed. Pre-departure cabin disinsection involves aerosol spraying after passengers have boarded but before the aircraft is pushed back for departure. This method is effective for a single flight sector and ensures all areas of the cabin, including the flight deck, open overhead lockers, coat lockers, and toilets, are treated. The spray must not be directed at smoke detectors or sensitive equipment, and any non-compliance with procedures must be reported to the intended first port before arrival. Certification of disinsection treatments is the responsibility of contracting states to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO). Airline operators must ensure certification meets the requirements of the arrival country. When both residual and aerosol disinsection treatments are applied, all relevant ICAO documentation must be completed. Copies of the ICAO residual disinsection certificate and the General Declaration must be accessible. Authorities may require all exterior doors and windows, including cargo hold doors, to remain closed until clearance is granted. Cargo holds also require disinsection. If previously treated with residual spray, additional procedures may not apply. Pre-departure cargo hold disinsection must be conducted manually after all cargo is loaded and just before the cargo hold door is closed. Aerosols must be discharged to ensure all parts of the hold are treated. In cases where permethrin-based products are not authorized, alternative insecticides such as d-phenothrin or 1R-trans-phenothrin aerosols may be used, subject to approval by the destination country. Used aerosol containers must remain in the hold for retrieval by ground handlers at the destination airport. When small animals are to be loaded, disinsection must occur before the animals are loaded but after all other cargo is on board. Procedures must align with the International Air Transport Association (IATA) and World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) regulations. Aerosols must be discharged to ensure complete coverage of the hold, and sensitive equipment must not be directly sprayed. The aircraft’s air-conditioning system must remain off during and for five minutes after spraying. Recirculation fans may remain on if essential but should be set to the lowest rate. Any non-compliance with procedures must be reported to the intended first port before arrival.
